entry.summary: An agent endpoint returns HTTP 200 in 99.95% of requests. The service is “up.” Meanwhile, some successful responses skip retrieval, some tool calls exceed their budget, and a few write actions occur without the expected approval. Availability is healthy while the product is not. Traditional service-level indicators still matter. That target should describe what users need, not whatever metric is easiest to collect. For an agent, “successful request” is too ambiguous. Split the promise into distinct indicator families. entry.title: Why I Got Tired of 3 AM False Alarms and Built a Multi-Region Synthetic Monitoring Platform
entry.summary: Every engineer on call knows the dread of an alert blaring at 3:17 AM. You stumble out of bed, pry open your laptop with one eye open, SSH into production, check CPU graphs, pull container logs, and test the endpoint—only to realize: Everything is running completely fine. The incident wasn't an outage. It was a single probe node in a single cloud datacenter suffering a transient BGP route flap, a 2-second DNS timeout, or an ISP blip. Yet, your uptime monitor treated it as catastrophic downtime, dialed your phone, and shattered your sleep. After dealing with alert fatigue and false alarms across multiple teams, I decided to build a platform that solves this fundamental flaw: Pingava. Most legacy uptime monitors still operate on a primitive model: One server in one region sends an HTTP GET request every 60 seconds. If that single request times out or returns a non-200 status code, it immediately fires an alert. The reality of the public internet is messy. Transit providers hiccup, local peering links drop packets, and CDN edge caches experience micro-latency. A timeout observed in Virginia does not mean your users in London, Frankfurt, or Singapore are experiencing downtime. Treating single-node anomalies as global outages leads directly to alert fatigue—and alert fatigue is how real, critical outages get ignored. Acompanhar inflação e outros indicadores econômicos com gráficos. Acompanhar dívida pública e gastos governamentais. Consultar salários de autoridades e visualizar informações públicas relacionadas aos seus gastos. Criar gráficos e indicadores simples para facilitar a compreensão dos dados. Ampliar a integração para mais municípios e fontes de dados. A proposta é construir uma plataforma simples de monitoramento, comparação e visualização de dados públicos, permitindo que qualquer pessoa consiga entender melhor para onde o dinheiro público está indo. Quem tiver interesse em contribuir com código, ideias, dados, integrações, UX/UI ou melhorias na arquitetura será muito bem-vindo ao projeto.
